tldr:
**Few-shot examples** are the most reliable way to get **consistent format** and **judgment that generalises**:

- **2–4 targeted examples** (the docs say 3–5), wrapped in `<example>` tags.
- **Show every output field.**
- For ambiguous cases, show **why this action over the plausible alternative**.
- **Vary the examples**, so the model doesn't copy an unintended pattern.
- **Cover varied input formats**, so informal values aren't left null.

When **iterating**, share **specific test failures** (expected vs actual). Use the **interview pattern** in unfamiliar domains. Send **interacting** problems in **one** message, and independent ones one at a time.
mentalModel: Examples are worked solutions on the whiteboard: students copy their format exactly, and if you show your reasoning they can solve new problems — but if every worked example has the same answer, they learn the answer, not the method. And when marking homework, “wrong” teaches nothing; “question 3: expected 12, you wrote 21” does.
whatItIs:
The exam guide covers few-shot prompting (Guide §6 · TS 4.2, pp.16–17) and iterative refinement (TS 3.5, pp.14–15). The
docs' prompting best practices give the rules for examples. D4.1 covers explicit criteria (TS 4.1).

**Sub-concepts — each with its picture to remember**

| # | Sub-concept | 🧭 Mental model | ⭐ Exam reference |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Format examples | Students copy the worked solution's layout exactly. | ⭐ TS 4.2 · Knowledge 1, Skill 2 |
| 2 | Ambiguous-case examples with reasoning | Show the working, not just the answer. | ⭐ TS 4.2 · Knowledge 2–3, Skill 1 |
| 3 | Diverse examples | If every example has the same answer, they learn the answer. | 📘 docs |
| 4 | Varied input formats | Worked examples in cm, feet and “about two metres”. | ⭐ TS 4.2 · Knowledge 4, Skill 5 |
| 5 | Concrete input/output examples | “This goes in, that comes out” beats a paragraph. | ⭐ TS 3.5 · Knowledge 1, Skill 1 |
| 6 | Test-driven iteration | Mark the homework: “Q3 expected 12, you wrote 21”. | ⭐ TS 3.5 · Knowledge 2, Skill 2 |
| 7 | Interview pattern | Let the new hire ask questions before building. | ⭐ TS 3.5 · Knowledge 3, Skill 3 |
| 8 | Together vs one at a time | Tangled knots are untied together; separate ones one by one. | ⭐ TS 3.5 · Knowledge 4, Skill 5 |

**Good examples** (docs + guide)

| # | Property | Why |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Relevant — mirror the real inputs | The model copies what it sees |
| 2 | Diverse — different outcomes and edge cases | Avoids unintended patterns (“always doc”) |
| 3 | Complete — every output field | Consistent format |
| 4 | Reasoned (for ambiguous cases) — why this over that | Judgment that generalises |
| 5 | Structured — in `<example>` / `<examples>` tags | Kept apart from instructions |
| 6 | A handful — guide 2–4, docs 3–5 | Enough to show the pattern |

**Iterating with Claude** (guide TS 3.5)

| # | Situation | Do | Don't |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Prose is read inconsistently | Give 2–3 concrete input → output examples | Rewrite the paragraph again |
| 2 | Building something testable | Write the tests first; share failures (expected vs actual) | “It doesn't work” |
| 3 | Unfamiliar domain | Interview pattern: let Claude ask about caching, failure modes, … first | Jump straight to code |
| 4 | Issues that interact | One detailed message covering all of them | Fix one, then the other |
| 5 | Independent issues | One at a time | — |
howItWorks:
1. **Inconsistent output?** Add 2–4 examples that show every field of the format you want.
2. **Ambiguous cases?** Make the examples show why one action beat the plausible alternative, and vary the outcomes.
3. **Extraction nulls?** Add examples covering the informal and varied formats you actually receive.
4. **Iterating on code?** Write tests first, then share the failures with expected vs actual. In unfamiliar territory, let
   Claude interview you first.
5. **Several problems?** If they interact, send them in one detailed message. If they're independent, fix them one at a time.

grounding.text: Make examples relevant (mirror the real use case), diverse (cover edge cases; vary enough that Claude doesn't pick up unintended patterns) and structured (wrap them in <example> / <examples> tags); 3–5 examples are suggested.

grounding.text: Few-shot examples are the most effective technique for consistently formatted, actionable output when instructions alone are inconsistent; they demonstrate ambiguous-case handling; they let the model generalise judgment to new patterns; they reduce hallucination in extraction (informal measurements, varied structures).

Skills: 2–4 targeted examples for ambiguous cases that show why one action beat plausible alternatives; examples of the exact output format (location, issue, severity, fix); examples distinguishing acceptable patterns from real issues; examples of varied document structures; examples with varied formats to fix empty/null required fields.

Iterative refinement: concrete input/output examples beat prose when descriptions are interpreted inconsistently; write tests first and iterate by sharing failures; the interview pattern (Claude asks questions first); describe interacting problems together, independent ones one at a time.

Skills: 2–3 concrete input/output examples; tests covering behaviour, edge cases and performance, then share failures; the interview pattern for unfamiliar domains; specific test cases with example input and expected output for edge cases; one detailed message for interacting issues.
The guide suggests 2–4 targeted examples (TS 4.2 S1); the docs suggest 3–5. Both agree on a handful of relevant, varied examples.

examPoints.text: Few-shot examples are the most effective way to get consistently formatted, actionable output when instructions alone are inconsistent.
Few-shot examples demonstrate how to handle ambiguous cases (e.g. tool selection).
Examples let the model generalise judgment to new patterns, not just match the listed cases.
Examples reduce hallucination in extraction (informal measurements, varied structures).
Write 2–4 targeted examples for ambiguous cases that show why one action beat plausible alternatives.
Include examples of the exact output format (location, issue, severity, suggested fix).
Include examples separating acceptable code patterns from real issues, to cut false positives while generalising.
Show correct handling of varied document structures (inline citations vs bibliographies).
Add examples with varied formats to fix empty/null extraction of required fields.
Concrete input/output examples communicate transformations best when prose is read inconsistently.
Test-driven iteration: write tests first, iterate by sharing failures.
The interview pattern: Claude asks questions to surface considerations before implementing.
Interacting problems in one message; independent problems one at a time.
Write tests for behaviour, edge cases and performance first, then share failures.
Address interacting issues in a single detailed message; iterate sequentially on independent ones.

labIntro:
You write the examples and the iteration choices. A **simulated** model follows deterministic stand-in rules, listed in
`utils/fewshot_lab.py`: it copies the format it's shown, generalises only from reasoned and varied examples, extracts informal
values only if it has seen varied formats, converges only on specific test feedback, and ping-pongs on interacting bugs fixed
separately.

variants.label: ✅ ⭐ format examples · reasoned, varied ambiguous-case examples · varied formats · specific test failures · interacting fixes together
variants.code:
from utils.fewshot_lab import SCENARIO, extract, fix, iterate, review, route   # SIMULATED model

# 1. Show the exact output format - every field, in every example
REVIEW_EXAMPLES = [
    {"input": "def total(items): return sum(i.price for i in items[:-1])",
     "output": {"location": "cart.py:57", "issue": "slice drops the last item", "severity": "major", "fix": "use items, not items[:-1]"}},
    {"input": "query = f\"SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '{name}'\"",
     "output": {"location": "search.py:21", "issue": "SQL built from user input", "severity": "critical", "fix": "use a parameterised query"}},
]

# 2. Ambiguous cases: show the REASONING - why this tool over the plausible alternative - with more than one outcome
ROUTING_EXAMPLES = [
    {"request": "Summarise these web search results about heat pumps", "tool": "web",
     "why": "the input is search results, so the web tool over the document tool, even though it says summarise"},
    {"request": "Pull the totals out of the attached PDF invoice", "tool": "doc",
     "why": "an attached file, so the document tool rather than the web tool"},
    {"request": "Turn these search results into a one-page brief", "tool": "web",
     "why": "search results again - the web tool, not the document tool, whatever the output format"},
]

# 3. Varied input formats, so informal values aren't left null
EXTRACT_EXAMPLES = [{"text": "about 1.8 metres", "height_m": 1.8}, {"text": "5 ft 11 in", "height_m": 1.80},
                    {"text": "172 cm", "height_m": 1.72}]


def feedback(failures):
    """Iterate by sharing the failing tests: name, expected, actual."""
    return "\n".join(f"{t['name']}: expected {t['expected']}, got {t['got']}" for t in failures)


FIX_TOGETHER = True   # the two bugs interact (tax relies on total()'s rounding) -> one detailed message

if SCENARIO == "format_consistency":
    review(REVIEW_EXAMPLES)
elif SCENARIO == "ambiguous_case":
    route(ROUTING_EXAMPLES)
elif SCENARIO == "informal_extraction":
    extract(EXTRACT_EXAMPLES)
elif SCENARIO == "test_driven":
    iterate(feedback)
else:
    fix(together=FIX_TOGETHER)
variants.observe: format_consistency: all three findings share location / issue / severity / fix. ambiguous_case: the new “news search results” request goes to the web tool — it generalised. informal_extraction: all four heights extracted. test_driven: passes after 2 rounds. interacting_issues: both bugs fixed in round 1.
variants.why: The examples show the format and the reasoning, the feedback names what failed, and interacting problems travel together.

questions.q: A CI review prompt lists the four fields every finding needs (location, issue, severity, suggested fix), but about 20% of findings come back in varying shapes that the comment bot can't post. Adding “follow the format exactly” in capitals changed nothing. What is the most effective fix?
opts: Add a few examples that show findings in exactly the required format.
Reshape the findings afterwards with a regex that fills the four fields.
Repeat the field list at the end of the prompt as well as at the start.
Ask the reviewer to double-check each finding's format before replying.
questions.explain: Few-shot examples are the most effective way to get consistent output formatting when instructions alone aren't enough. B patches the output after the fact. C and D repeat the instruction that already failed.

questions.q: A support agent hesitates between get_customer and lookup_order on requests like “it's about my last purchase”, choosing inconsistently in about 30% of such cases. Both tool descriptions were recently rewritten and work well for unambiguous requests. What is the best prompt addition?
opts: A rule at the top of the prompt saying “when unsure, always call lookup_order first”.
Twenty examples of clear-cut requests, so the model sees many correct tool choices together.
A confidence threshold below which the agent asks the customer which tool it should use.
Two to four targeted examples of ambiguous requests, each showing the chosen tool and why.
questions.explain: A few examples aimed at the ambiguous cases, each with its reasoning, teach the judgement that is missing. A hard-codes one answer for every ambiguous case. B spends examples on the cases that already work. C uses self-reported confidence and hands an internal choice to the customer.

questions.q: Every time the agent mishandles a new kind of ambiguous request, the team adds another rule to the prompt. After 30 rules, it still fails on about 12% of phrasings nobody anticipated, and some rules now contradict each other. What approach generalises better?
opts: Keep adding rules, but group them by topic so the model can find the relevant rule more easily.
A few well-chosen examples that show the reasoning, so the model can apply it to new patterns.
Replace the rules with one instruction to “use your best judgement on ambiguous requests”.
A classifier that detects ambiguous requests and routes them to a human before the agent sees them.
questions.explain: Examples that show the reasoning let the model generalise to new patterns, where rules only cover the cases someone thought of. A keeps chasing individual cases. C removes the guidance altogether. D is over-engineered and moves the ambiguity rather than resolving it.

questions.q: Extracting product dimensions, the pipeline returns null for required measurements in about 18% of documents. All of these use informal wording like “about two metres” or “a shade under 50cm”, while formal measurements such as “200 cm” are extracted correctly. What is the best fix?
opts: Make the measurement fields optional, so informal documents stop failing schema validation.
Add a regex pre-processing step that converts informal phrases into numbers before extraction.
Add examples covering varied and informal ways of writing measurements, with correct extraction.
Tell the model in the prompt to “extract any measurements even when they are written informally”.
questions.explain: Examples covering the varied ways a value is written reduce nulls on informal inputs. A hides the failure behind nulls. B needs a pattern for every phrasing. D is an instruction without the demonstration that makes it work.

questions.q: The CI reviewer flags the team's standard retry decorator as “unsafe error handling” on about 10 PRs a week, while also missing real cases of swallowed exceptions. The prompt currently says “flag unsafe error handling”. What is the most effective prompt change?
opts: A rule saying “never flag decorators”, so the retry decorator stops appearing in the findings.
Examples contrasting the acceptable decorator pattern with genuinely swallowed exceptions.
A longer definition of “unsafe error handling” that lists every exception type it may involve.
Removing the error-handling checks, since the reviewer can't tell good cases from bad ones.
questions.explain: Examples that contrast an acceptable pattern with a real issue teach the distinction, which fixes both the false positives and the misses. A creates a blind spot for bad decorators. C adds length but not the contrast. D gives up on real bugs.

questions.q: A citation extractor works on papers with a bibliography at the end, but misses or duplicates citations in about 40% of papers that cite inline, such as (Author, 2021), with no bibliography. All three of its few-shot examples are bibliography-style papers. What is the best fix?
opts: Add a rule telling the model to look for inline citations whenever a paper has no bibliography.
Pre-process inline-citation papers by generating a bibliography for them before extraction starts.
Add examples showing correct extraction from both structures: inline citations and bibliographies.
Send inline-citation papers to a separate pipeline that uses a larger model for the extraction.
questions.explain: The examples cover only one document structure. Adding examples of the other structure is the fix. A states the goal without demonstrating it. B adds a fragile pre-processing step. D throws a bigger model at a gap in the examples.

questions.q: A developer describes in prose how Claude Code should convert API field names: snake_case to camelCase, but keep “ID” uppercase and leave “_links” alone. Across 5 runs the interpretation differs each time, and user_id has become userId, userID and userIdentifier. What communicates the transformation best?
opts: Two or three concrete input-to-output examples, including the exceptions.
A longer prose description that spells out every rule in more detail.
A regular expression that describes the whole pattern, pasted into the prompt.
A reminder at the end of the prompt to follow the rules exactly as written.
questions.explain: Concrete input/output examples are the most effective way to communicate a transformation when prose is read inconsistently. B adds more of what failed. C can't easily express the exceptions. D repeats the instruction.

questions.q: A developer asks Claude Code to fix a data migration script and replies “still broken” after each attempt. After 7 rounds, the script handles two of the four known edge cases, and a different one breaks each time. What is the more effective way to iterate?
opts: Keep replying “still broken”, but ask Claude to try a completely different approach each round.
Paste the whole database schema into the conversation, so Claude has the full context to work with.
Ask Claude to list every edge case it can think of before it attempts another fix to the script.
Write tests for the expected behaviour and edge cases first, then share the specific failures.
questions.explain: Test-driven iteration defines “done”, and each specific failure tells Claude exactly what to fix. A gives no information. B adds context but not the definition of success. C guesses at edge cases the developer already knows.

questions.q: A developer who has never built a caching layer asks Claude Code to add one to an API serving about 2,000 requests a second. They aren't sure what they haven't thought of, and a previous attempt served stale prices for an hour. What is the best way to start?
opts: Ask Claude to implement a standard cache with a 60-second TTL, and adjust it after deployment.
Have Claude interview them first about invalidation, failure modes and consistency needs.
Copy a caching layer from another service, and ask Claude to adapt it to this API's code.
Start in plan mode and ask Claude for a design, without discussing any requirements first.
questions.explain: In an unfamiliar domain, having Claude ask questions first brings out considerations the developer hasn't anticipated, such as invalidation. A repeats the stale-data risk. C imports someone else's assumptions. D plans without the requirements.

questions.q: A migration script generated by Claude Code crashes on rows where middle_name is null, about 3% of 2 million rows. The developer's bug report, “it fails on some names”, produced a fix that didn't help. What is the most effective next message?
opts: A request to wrap the whole migration in try/except so that any failing rows are simply skipped.
The full stack trace, with no sample data, and a request to fix the error it shows.
Test cases with sample input rows, including a null middle_name, and the exact expected output.
A note that the problem is urgent, asking Claude to look more carefully at the name handling.
questions.explain: Specific test cases, with example inputs and the expected outputs, pin down the behaviour to fix. A hides the problem by skipping rows. B shows where it crashed but not what should happen. D adds urgency, not information.

questions.q: Three bugs are open: the tax calculation depends on how the order total is rounded, and both are wrong; a third bug, a typo in an email template, is unrelated. Fixing the rounding alone last week broke the tax totals. How should the developer raise them with Claude Code?
opts: The rounding and tax bugs together in one detailed message, and the typo separately.
All three in one single message, so that Claude sees every open problem at the same time.
Each bug in its own message, one after another, starting with the rounding bug.
The tax bug first, then the rounding bug once the tax fix has been verified.
questions.explain: Interacting problems belong in one message so the fixes are designed together. Independent ones are raised separately. B mixes an unrelated fix in with them. C and D split the interacting pair, which is what broke the tax totals last week.

faq.a: The guide says 2–4 targeted examples for ambiguous scenarios; the docs suggest 3–5. Both mean a handful of relevant, varied examples, not dozens.

faq.q: Won't examples make Claude copy them too literally?
faq.a: It can, if they're all alike. The docs' answer is diversity: vary the outcomes and edge cases so no unintended pattern stands out. Reasoning in the examples helps the model take the method, not the surface.
Before implementing in an unfamiliar area, ask Claude to question you: about cache invalidation, failure modes, edge cases. It surfaces considerations you hadn't planned for (TS 3.5).
